quirks: Norwegian church (Lutheran) marriage records are the primary genealogical source; the Evangelical Lutheran Church kept vital records as an arm of the national government throughout this period.
Parish (prestegjeld/sokn) must be identified before most searches — church records are organized at parish level, not county level. Identify the parish from a census, baptism, or other record first.
Couples were traditionally married in the bride's home parish, not the groom's — search the bride's parish (Unna Halsteinsdatter's father Halstein's parish) if the groom's parish yields nothing.

Patronymic naming convention: sons took father's first name + '-sen'; daughters took father's first name + '-datter'. 'Monsen' = son of Mons; 'Halsteinsdatter' = daughter of Halstein. These were not hereditary surnames — the same person appears under different 'surnames' in different record types. Fixed hereditary surnames became mandatory only with the Norwegian Naming Act of 1923.

Records written in Norwegian (Bokmål/Dano-Norwegian); earlier 19th-century records may use Danish orthography. Genealogical word list needed: 'viede/vigde/copulerede' = married; 'ungkarl' = bachelor; 'pige' = maiden; 'enkemand/enke' = widower/widow.
After 1830, Norwegian marriage records typically include fathers' names and birthplaces of both parties — critical for distinguishing individuals sharing a patronymic.
A standard printed format for parish registers was introduced in 1814, providing more structured fields including ages/birth dates, bondsmen, and marriage date.

The FamilySearch 'Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926' (collection 1468080) is index-only with no images — it is a legacy partial index. Confirm any hit with the original register via 'Norway, Church Books, 1797-1958' (collection 4237104) which has both index and 1,288,153 images, or via Digitalarkivet (digitalarkivet.no) which provides index & images.
Digitalarkivet (digitalarkivet.no) is the Norwegian national digital archive and the most comprehensive source for church records — free, with index and scanned images for most parishes.

No civil registration for genealogical purposes until 1876 (statistics only, not publicly available); Folkeregistre (community vital registers) began only in 1915. Church records are the sole source for marriages throughout the 19th century.

Volume search returned 21,761 total digitized volumes for Norway in marriage/religious record types (1800-1920); the vast majority are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — they must be browsed image by image unless found through the indexed collections or Digitalarkivet.
The county administrative unit was called 'amt' before 1917 and renamed 'fylke' in 1917; some records may be filed under the older 'amt' designation in older finding aids.

Norway has 20 historical counties (fylker/amt); each is subdivided into parishes. Once a parish is identified, search the county-level FamilySearch Wiki page (e.g., https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Hedmark_County,_Norway_Genealogy) for parish-specific collections and digitization status.

# Locality Guide: Norway (1800–1920)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Country:** Norway, Scandinavia, Northern Europe
- **Administrative divisions:** Counties (*amt*, renamed *fylke* in 1917) → parishes (*prestegjeld/sokn*)
- **Political status:** Union with Denmark ended 1814; union with Sweden (United Kingdoms of Sweden and Norway) 1814–1905; fully independent 1905
- **Population during period:** ~900,000 (1800) → ~2.6 million (1920) [Gapminder/Populstat estimates]
- **Religion:** Evangelical Lutheran (state church from 1536 Reformation); church kept all vital records as arm of national government
- **Language of records:** Norwegian (Bokmål/Dano-Norwegian); earlier 19th-century records may use Danish orthography
- **Naming customs:** Patronymic system throughout most of the 19th century — sons took father's first name + *-sen*; daughters took father's first name + *-datter*. These changed with each generation. Fixed hereditary surnames mandated only from 1923 (Norwegian Naming Act).

## Boundary changes
- County unit called *amt* until 1917, renamed *fylke* in 1917; several counties also renamed at that time
- Boundaries otherwise stable within the period; some parishes were subdivided as populations grew
- For pre-1814 context: records created under Danish-Norwegian administration

## Available record types

### Church records (primary source)
- **Denominations:** Evangelical Lutheran (state church — covers essentially the entire population)
- **Record types:** Baptisms (*fødte/døbte*), confirmations (*konfirmerede*), marriages (*viede/vigde/copulerede*), burials (*døde/begravede*), moving in/out lists (*tilgangs-/avgangslister*)
- **Marriage record content:**
  - Names of bride and groom, marriage date, ages/status (bachelor/widower; maiden/widow), occupations, place(s) of residence
  - Names of bondsmen (witnesses who confirmed eligibility to marry — often fathers)
  - Engagement (*trolovelse*) date and banns (announced 3 consecutive Sundays before wedding) in earlier records
  - After ~1830: fathers' names and birthplaces of both parties routinely included
  - Printed standard format introduced 1814 (used more consistently from then on)
  - Couples traditionally married in the **bride's home parish**
- **Start dates:** Records vary by parish; church not keeping records across entire country until 1688. Earliest parish register in Norway is 1623 (Andebu, Vestfold). Standard format in use from 1814.
- **Language:** Norwegian/Dano-Norwegian; Latin terms appear in older records
- **Where held:** Originals in regional state archives (*statsarkivene*); scanned images at Digitalarkivet and FamilySearch

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date (statistical):** 1876 — law required births, marriages, deaths submitted to the Central Bureau of Statistics; **not available to the public and not genealogically useful**
- **Start date (community registers):** 1915 — *Folkeregistre* (Registers of Vital Statistics) begun at community level; registration mandatory in all districts from 1946
- **Implication:** For the 19th century and until 1915, church records are the only vital records. There is no parallel civil marriage register for the period a Norwegian marriage in the 1800s would fall.

### Census records
- **1801:** Nationwide nominative census — indexed & images on FamilySearch (collection 3733603) and Ancestry
- **1865:** Nationwide nominative census — indexed & images on FamilySearch (collection 3756102)
- **1870:** Partial census — indexed & images on FamilySearch (collection 4135961)
- **1875:** Nationwide census — indexed only on FamilySearch (collection 1529106)
- **1891:** Nationwide census — indexed & images on FamilySearch (collection 4067726)
- **1900:** Nationwide census — indexed & images on FamilySearch (collection 3744863)
- **1910:** Available on MyHeritage and Ancestry (index only)
- All censuses also available at Digitalarkivet with index & images
- Census records will show household composition, ages, occupations, and places of birth — critical for identifying which parish the family belonged to

### Probate records
- **FamilySearch:** Norway, Probate Index Cards, 1640–1903 (collection 1661306) — 1,058,029 records, index only
- **Digitalarkivet:** Full probate records with images
- Probate (*skifte*) records list heirs and can confirm family relationships

### Land and farm records
- Norway has a unique *bygdebøker* (farm history books) tradition — compiled local histories listing all known residents of each farm across generations; excellent for placing a family in a specific parish
- Farm records (*matrikkel*) at Digitalarkivet

### Military records
- Conscription/muster rolls available for 19th century; held at state archives and Digitalarkivet

### Emigration records
- Large-scale emigration from Norway to America began ~1825 and accelerated after 1860
- Norway, Emigration Records, 1874–1960 (Ancestry)
- Norway, Emigration Registers, 1867–1973 (MyHeritage)
- Emigration indexes at Digitalarkivet

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Key collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Norway, Marriages, 1660–1926 (index only, 1.3M records); Norway, Church Books, 1797–1958 (index + images, 14.4M records); Baptisms, Burials, all Censuses | Free |
| Digitalarkivet (digitalarkivet.no) | Full church registers (index & images), all censuses, court records, probate, land records — most comprehensive source | Free |
| Ancestry | Norway Marriages 1660–1926; Baptisms; Burials; multiple censuses | Subscription |
| MyHeritage | Norway Marriages 1660–1926; Baptisms; Burials; censuses 1891/1900/1910 | Subscription |
| Norwegian Historical Data Centre (rhd.uit.no) | Parish record search, census indexes 1865–1910 | Free |
| Norway Heritage (norwayheritage.com) | Emigrant ship indexes | Free |

**Coverage note:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 21,761 digitized volumes matching marriage/religious record types for Norway 1800–1920. The first page (50 volumes sampled) shows the vast majority are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only. The indexed collections (1468080, 4237104) and Digitalarkivet are the efficient entry points.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives of Norway (Riksarkivet), Oslo | Central government records, national collections | In-person / online via Digitalarkivet |
| Regional State Archives (*statsarkivene*, 7 locations) | Original parish registers, probate, land records for their regions | In-person / scanned at Digitalarkivet |
| Local municipal archives | Folkeregistre (from 1915), local records | In-person / inquiry |

## Records NOT online
- Some rural and remote parish registers not yet fully scanned or indexed on FamilySearch (covered on Digitalarkivet but may require browsing)
- Folkeregistre community registers (post-1915) are restricted and not publicly accessible online
- Some clerical archives (marriage bann records, pastoral correspondence) exist at Digitalarkivet but may require knowing the specific parish

## Known record losses
- No major nationwide record destruction events reported for Norwegian church records; coverage is generally excellent
- Individual parish registers vary in survival; check Digitalarkivet for gaps within a specific parish

## Research tips
- **Identify the parish first.** Church records are organized at parish level. A census hit (especially 1865, 1875, 1891, or 1900) will give the parish of residence, which is the key to finding the marriage register. ([Norway Getting Started](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Getting_Started))
- **Search the bride's parish for the marriage.** Norwegian custom placed the marriage ceremony in the bride's home parish — if searching for Anders Monsen's marriage, Unna Halsteinsdatter's father Halstein's parish is the likely location of the register entry. ([Norway Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Church_Records#Marriages_(Viede,_Vigde,_Copulerede)))
- **Start with FamilySearch Norway, Marriages, 1660–1926 (collection 1468080)** for a quick name-index search, but treat it as a partial legacy index — verify every hit with the original image in Norway, Church Books, 1797–1958 (collection 4237104) or Digitalarkivet.
- **Digitalarkivet is the definitive source** for Norwegian church records — free, with images. URL: https://www.digitalarkivet.no/
- **Patronymic name variation:** 'Monsen' and 'Halsteinsdatter' are generational names, not fixed surnames. In later records (post-1923) the family may appear under a fixed farm name or adopted surname. Search census records first to anchor the family in a parish and confirm the name forms used.
- **After 1830 marriage records include fathers' names** — essential for distinguishing Anders Monsen (son of Mons) from other men named Anders Monsen in the same period.
- **Read the Norwegian Genealogical Word List** before reading original records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norwegian_Genealogical_Word_List
- **Bygdebøker (farm books)** are invaluable if the family's farm/place name is known — they reconstruct farm resident lists across generations and can pin the family to a specific location and time. ([Norway Farm Books](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Farm_Books))

entry.rationale: FamilySearch 'Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926' (collection 1468080) is the fastest indexed entry point: 1,330,979 records searchable by name at the country level, no parish identification required. Search for groom 'Anders Monsen' (father 'Mons') and bride 'Unna Halsteinsdatter' (father 'Halstein'). Try spelling variants: bride's name as 'Una', 'Unni', 'Unnæ'; patronymic as 'Holsteinsdatter', 'Halsteinsdtr'. Caution: this is a legacy partial index (assembled 2010, no additions since); a hit must be verified in the original image; a nil result does not rule out the marriage. Delivers: marriage date, parish, and parties' details if found.

FamilySearch 'Norway, Church Books, 1797-1958' (collection 4237104) is the most complete FamilySearch source: 14,398,439 records with 1,288,153 images, covering baptisms, confirmations, marriages, and burials. Search here to (a) verify any hit from pli_001 against the original image, and (b) broaden the search if pli_001 returns nothing — this collection supersedes the legacy marriage index in coverage. The full image allows reading all columns of the marriage entry: date, parties' names and ages, residence, fathers' names (standard after 1830), bondsmen/witnesses, and any remarks. Record the full contents per the objective's 'what does the record show?' requirement.

Digitalarkivet (https://www.digitalarkivet.no) is the Norwegian national digital archive — the most comprehensive source for Norwegian church records, free, with both index and scanned images for most parishes. It holds records that FamilySearch collections may not yet cover, and provides the highest-resolution original images. Search the marriage/church register index for 'Anders Monsen' and 'Unna Halsteinsdatter'. If the specific parish is known from earlier steps, browse that parish's marriage register directly. Delivers: original register image with all recorded fields.

Norwegian censuses 1865 (collection 3756102), 1875 (1529106), 1891 (4067726), and 1900 (3744863) are all indexed and searchable on FamilySearch at country level. Search for 'Anders Monsen' and 'Unna' (or 'Una') across these years. A census hit provides: (a) the parish/municipality of residence — the key to targeted marriage register searches; (b) ages (to bracket the marriage year); (c) household composition confirming the couple. The 1865 and 1875 censuses are particularly useful if the marriage occurred before those dates. The 1891 and 1900 censuses would show the established household. Census is a secondary source for the marriage date but a primary source for the parish.

FAN item: search FamilySearch 'Norway, Baptisms, 1634-1927' (collection 1467014, 5,277,294 records) for children baptized to Anders Monsen and Unna (Halsteinsdatter). Norwegian baptism records name both parents; a child's baptism entry places the family in a specific parish and often names the parents' residence and occupation. This item serves two purposes: (1) it identifies the parish of family residence after the marriage, enabling a targeted search of that parish's marriage register; (2) it corroborates the couple's identities and the approximate marriage date by working back from the first child's birth. Search for father 'Anders Monsen' with mother 'Unna' or 'Una'.

Full-text co-occurrence search (via search-full-text skill) across the full Norway church book corpus for the surname pair 'Monsen' + 'Halsteinsdatter' appearing on the same register page. This targets the AI-transcribed page text of unindexed or partially-indexed registers that name-indexed searches miss. The rare patronymic 'Halsteinsdatter' (daughter of Halstein) is distinctive and should return a small, manageable result set when paired with 'Monsen'. Execute as an unscoped co-occurrence search across all Norway records, not limited to a single collection id. Fallback for pli_001 and pli_002 when indexed searches return no result.

Ancestry 'Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926' (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/60095) indexes the same base data as FamilySearch collection 1468080 but with Ancestry's search interface and potentially additional transcriptions. Try if FamilySearch marriage index (pli_001) returns nothing — Ancestry's indexing and spelling-variant matching differ and may surface an entry missed there. Paid subscription required. Fallback for pli_001.

entry.rationale: Digitalarkivet church book browser (https://media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse) is the primary source for Hamre parish marriage registers 1760-1800. Hamre parish (historical municipality Hammer, Hordaland, renamed 1915) is the most probable location: Anders Monsen was christened at Hamre kirke 7 April 1759 (QKQ1-3QH) and Unna Halsteinsdatter was christened at Hamre 27 May 1745. Norwegian custom places a marriage in the bride's parish. The 1963 LDS family group sheet (src_001) confirmed the family group at Hamre, Hordaland. FamilySearch indexed collections (pli_001, pli_002) and FTS (pli_006) were all negative — the marriage is in an un-indexed original image. Digitalarkivet holds the Hamre ministerialbok (church register) images. Estimated marriage year: 1775-1790 (Anders aged 16-31; Unna aged 30-45). Requires interactive user capture (bot-protected).

The 1801 Norway census (FamilySearch collection 1569427) was NOT searched in pli_004, which covered only 1865-1900. Anders Monsen (born 1759) and Unna Halsteinsdatter (born 1745) were both alive in 1801 (ages 42 and 56 respectively; Anders died in 1821). A household listing would: (1) confirm the couple lived together and were married; (2) identify their parish of residence, enabling a targeted Digitalarkivet search; (3) name any children, allowing backward triangulation to the marriage year. This is the only fully autonomous search in this plan — country-level indexed census search on FamilySearch. Search for 'Anders Monsen' in Norway, 1801.

FAN item — Unna Halsteinsdatter's own baptism record has never been directly searched in this project. Unna was christened 27 May 1745 at Hamre (from tree.gedcomx.json), but that fact lacks a source citation in this research project. Her baptism register entry would name her parents, directly confirming or denying that Halstein Johannesen is her father — the key inference from src_001 that 'Una' = 'Unna Halsteinsdatter, daughter of Halstein'. Search FamilySearch 'Norway, Baptisms, 1634-1927' (collection 1467014) for 'Unna' baptized ~May 1745 in Hammer/Hamre parish, father 'Halstein Johannesen'. A confirmed parentage link strengthens the identity case and may also name Unna's mother (needed for full family reconstruction). Date window sized to Unna's birth decade.

Fallback for pli_008 (Hamre/Hammer parish browse). Hosanger parish is adjacent to Hamre in Hordaland and was explicitly named alongside Hamre in the FTS result (log_028, collection M9J1-LMH) as a location associated with the Halstein Johannesen family. If the Hamre marriage register does not contain the entry, Hosanger is the next most likely parish. Access via Digitalarkivet church book browser (https://media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse), browsing Hosanger prosti, Hordaland. Requires interactive user capture (bot-protected).

entry.narrative_markdown:
## When and Where Did Anders Monsen Marry Unna Halsteinsdatter? — Proof Summary (Not Proved)

### Research Question

This summary addresses the question: When and where did Anders Monsen, son of Mons Monsen, marry Unna Halsteinsdatter?

### Conclusion

The date and place of the marriage between Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter **cannot be established from the evidence gathered to date**. The current evidence is insufficient to answer either element of the question with any precision. The conclusion is *not proved* — not because a negative conclusion is warranted, but because the decisive source (the Hamre parish marriage register, held at Digitalarkivet) has not yet been searched. This summary documents the interim state of research and identifies the next required step.

### Sources Consulted and Their Classification

Two sources contributed evidence to this question.

**Source 1: 1963 LDS Family Group Sheet (derivative/secondary/indirect)**

An LDS-compiled family group sheet submitted to the Genealogical Society of Utah in 1963 and now accessible through FamilySearch as a document-image record identifies "Anders Monsen" and "Una" alongside members of a "Halsteinsen" family — Johannes, Magdali, Ole, Jens, and Martha Halsteinsen — under the household of "Halstein Johannesen" at Hamre, Hordaland, Norway.[^1] This document is classified as *derivative* (compiled by an unknown researcher from sources not disclosed), *secondary* (reconstructing events from the 1700s–1800s two centuries after the fact, by an informant of unknown proximity), and *indirect* as evidence of the marriage (the document establishes a family-group association but states no marriage date or place). The physical image was not examined; the assertions above derive from a FamilySearch full-text search stub, and the image may contain additional detail not captured here.

Notwithstanding these limitations, the source is meaningful corroboration: the name "Una" appearing in the wife role alongside "Halstein Johannesen's" children is consistent with the expected patronymic form "Unna Halsteinsdatter" (daughter of Halstein). The place association, Hamre, Hordaland, aligns with Unna's known christening at Hamre kirke on 27 May 1745 and with Anders Monsen's own christening at Hamre kirke on 7 April 1759. Taken together, the source provides modest circumstantial corroboration that this couple was associated with Hamre, Hordaland, but it establishes neither the date nor the place of their marriage.

**Source 2: Norway Census, 1801 (original/indeterminate/direct and negative)**

The 1801 Norway census — a government enumeration carried out on a fixed date — records Anders Monsen as head of household at Hamre, Hordaland, with household members Nils Andersen (born ca. 1787), Kari Andersdatter (born ca. 1784), and Borni Nilsdatter (born ca. 1744).[^2] The census is an *original* record. The birth-year data for Anders (ca. 1758, derived from a stated age by FamilySearch indexers) is *indeterminate* information, while the residence and household-composition data is *primary* information provided by a government enumerator as direct witness.

Significantly, **Unna Halsteinsdatter is entirely absent from this household**. A wife would ordinarily appear in her husband's census household; her absence is negative evidence. The most likely explanation is that Unna predeceased 1801, though enumeration omission or a temporary absence cannot be entirely excluded. This negative evidence establishes one firm bracket: **if Anders and Unna were married, the marriage occurred before 1801**. It does not establish when or where the marriage occurred.

### Correlation and Weight of Evidence

The two sources agree in situating Anders Monsen and his family at Hamre, Hordaland. The 1963 LDS sheet associates him with Unna in a Halstein Johannesen family context; the 1801 census confirms his continued presence at Hamre. Norwegian custom placed marriage in the bride's home parish; Unna Halsteinsdatter's christening at Hamre kirke on 27 May 1745 makes Hamre the most probable locus of the marriage.

The correlated evidence supports a *possible* conclusion that the marriage occurred in Hamre, Hordaland, sometime before 1801, but this falls well short of establishing the specific date or place the question asks for. No source consulted contains a marriage date, a marriage place, a bondsman entry, or any other characteristic marker of a Norwegian church marriage record.

### Scope of Searches Conducted

The following record collections were searched and returned no marriage record for this couple:

- FamilySearch, *Norway, Marriages, 1660–1926* (collection 1468080) — searched across seven name variants; all negative. This collection is index-only (no images) and is a partial legacy index.
- FamilySearch, *Norway, Church Books, 1797–1958* (collection 4237104) — searched from both groom and bride perspectives; all negative. Coverage for Hamre parish in the late 18th century may be incomplete on this platform.
- FamilySearch Norway census collections (1801, 1865, 1875, 1891, 1900) — 1801 located Anders at Hamre; all others negative. No children of Anders and Unna were identified to triangulate a marriage date.
- FamilySearch baptism searches for children of Anders Monsen (five variants) — all negative.
- FamilySearch full-text co-occurrence searches (five queries) — geographic context confirmed but no marriage record found. Norwegian church books for the 18th century are not in the full-text-searchable corpus.
- Unna Halsteinsdatter's baptism (five search variants on FamilySearch) — all negative; Hamre records for the 1740s are unindexed on FamilySearch.

### Critical Gap: Digitalarkivet Unsearched

The single most decisive unsearched source is the **Hamre parish marriage register for approximately 1760–1800**, held at Digitalarkivet (digitalarkivet.no), the Norwegian national digital archive. Norwegian custom placed marriage in the bride's home parish; Hamre is confirmed as Unna Halsteinsdatter's christening parish, making the Hamre kirkebøk the expected location of the marriage entry. Digitalarkivet is a free public digital archive providing indexed and scanned images of most Norwegian parish registers; it was not accessed in this research cycle because interactive browser navigation was unavailable in autonomous research mode. This is a tool-transport limitation, not a legal seal, record destruction, or privacy embargo — the source is publicly accessible.

A secondary fallback is Hosanger parish (Hordaland), which would apply if Unna's family was resident there rather than Hamre at the time of the marriage. Ancestry Norway Marriages was also not searched.

Because these sources remain unsearched, research exhaustiveness cannot be declared, and the question cannot be closed. The marriage date and place remain **not established from the evidence gathered to date** — a claim about the current record set, not about the fact itself.

### Next Step

The required next step is a user-assisted browse of the Digitalarkivet Hamre parish marriage register, ca. 1760–1800, for an entry naming Anders Monsen and/or Unna Halsteinsdatter (or variant spellings). The Norwegian marriage-record search term is *viede*, *vigde*, or *copulerede* in 18th-century Dano-Norwegian. A positive result would likely establish both the date and the place, and would upgrade this conclusion. If the Hamre register is negative, the Hosanger fallback should be searched next.

[^2]: "Norges folketelling, 1801 [Norway Census, 1801]," FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:8YMV-R76Z : accessed 9 September 2026), entry for Anders Monsen, Hamre, Hordaland.

fields.narrative_markdown:
## When and Where Did Anders Monsen Marry Unna Halsteinsdatter? — Proof Summary (Probable)

### Research Question

This summary addresses the question: When and where did Anders Monsen, son of Mons Monsen, marry Unna Halsteinsdatter?

### Conclusion

The preponderance of available evidence establishes that Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter (also rendered as Una) were most probably married on **25 June 1786** in **Hamre parish, Hordaland, Norway**. The conclusion rests on a derivative source that explicitly states the date and cites a specific original parish register, corroborated by independent negative evidence from the 1801 Norway census. No contradicting evidence has been found. Because the underlying original church record (Hamre Parish Records, film 17885) has not been independently verified, and because Digitalarkivet has not been searched, the conclusion is assessed at **probable** rather than proved.

### Sources Consulted and Their Classification

**Source 1: 1963 LDS Family Group Sheet, Ivar Martin Floisand (derivative/secondary/direct)**

A Family Group Sheet submitted to the Genealogical Society of Utah in 1963 by Ivar Martin Floisand — identified in the document as a 4th great-grandson of Halstein Johannesen — and now accessible through FamilySearch as a digital image[^1] explicitly lists Unna (Una) Halsteinsdatter as child #2 of Halstein Johannesen, born 29 May 1745, and records her marriage to Anders Monsen on 25 June 1786. The submitter's citation on the sheet reads: "Hamre Parish Records, F. Norw, Hordald, H1 Pt 1, film 17885."

This source is classified as *derivative* (a compiled Family Group Sheet, not the original church register), *secondary* information (Ivar Martin Floisand was an informant approximately 200 years removed from the event and not present at the marriage), and *direct* evidence of the marriage date (the date 25 June 1786 is explicitly stated, not inferred). The submitter's acknowledged access to the microfilm of the Hamre parish register (film 17885) substantially enhances the reliability of this derivative source: the stated date is likely a transcription from the original rather than a family memory or unsourced tradition. The place of marriage is not explicitly named on the marriage line of the FGS but is implied by the source's scope — the Hamre Parish Records cited by the submitter — and by the family's documented Hamre parish context (Unna's christening at Hamre kirke on 27 May 1745; Anders Monsen's christening at Hamre kirke on 7 April 1759).

The source also identifies five siblings of Unna: Johannes, Magdali, Ole, Jens, and Martha Halsteinsen — all consistent with the patronymic convention (children of Halstein) and with no internal inconsistency. The document's internal coherence and the submitter's cited access to the original film are the primary bases for assessing this source above mere "possible."

**Source 2: Norway Census, 1801 (original/primary-for-residence/negative evidence)**

The 1801 Norway census records Anders Monsen as head of household at Hamre, Hordaland, with household members Nils Andersen (born ca. 1787), Kari Andersdatter (born ca. 1784), and Borni Nilsdatter (born ca. 1744).[^2] The census is an *original* record; residence and household-composition data constitute *primary* information recorded by a government enumerator as a contemporary witness. Unna Halsteinsdatter is entirely absent from this household. This negative evidence from an original, independent source provides two corroborating inferences: (1) any marriage between Anders and Unna necessarily predated 1801, which is consistent with the 1786 date stated in the FGS; and (2) Unna most likely predeceased 1801, suggesting the marriage had run its full course before that date.

### Correlation of Evidence

The two sources are independent of each other and agree in their respective bearing on the question. The 1963 FGS directly states the marriage date as 25 June 1786 and traces it to a specific film of the Hamre parish records. The 1801 census independently places Anders Monsen at Hamre without a wife present, consistent with a marriage in 1786 to a woman who likely died before 1801. No source in the evidentiary base contradicts the 25 June 1786 date or suggests any alternative. The geographic coherence — both parties christened at Hamre kirke, family records centered on Hamre, Hordaland — further supports the implied marriage place of Hamre parish.

Unna's birth date from the FGS (29 May 1745) differs by two days from the existing tree entry for her christening (27 May 1745). This minor discrepancy is consistent with a likely conflation of birth date and christening date in the FGS — an extremely common occurrence in compiled genealogies — and does not undermine the source's reliability for the marriage date.

### Limitations and Gaps

The conclusion carries two significant limitations.

First, the marriage date of 25 June 1786 derives from a single derivative source. The source cites the Hamre parish records on film 17885 but is not itself the original. Independent verification against the original Hamre kirkebøk at Digitalarkivet has not been completed; this search was unavailable in autonomous mode because Digitalarkivet requires interactive browser navigation. This is a tool-transport limitation, not a legal seal or destruction of the record. A search of Digitalarkivet could confirm the date, disclose a variant date, or reveal that the entry was not found — any of which would affect the conclusion.

Second, the marriage place is not explicitly stated in the FGS for this marriage line; it is inferred from the source's Hamre parish scope and the parties' documented association with Hamre. Norwegian custom placed marriage in the bride's home parish, which for Unna Halsteinsdatter is Hamre. The implied place is consistent with all available evidence, but no direct statement of the marriage place has been found.

Neither limitation contradicts the existing evidence; both are gaps in corroboration. The conclusion is therefore assessed at *probable* — the evidence preponderates toward 25 June 1786, Hamre parish, but lacks the original-record verification and research exhaustiveness required for the proved standard.

### GPS Component Assessment

- **Component 1 (Exhaustive research):** Not fully met. Digitalarkivet (the Hamre parish marriage register ca. 1760–1800) has not been searched. The conclusion is at probable, not proved, in part because of this gap.
- **Component 2 (Complete citations):** The derivative source cites a specific film (17885) of the Hamre Parish Records. The original microfilm has not been independently consulted; citations trace to the FGS and the 1801 census.
- **Component 3 (Analysis and correlation):** Met. Both sources are classified across all three evidence dimensions; they are independent and consistent.
- **Component 4 (Conflict resolution):** Met. No conflicts exist in the evidentiary base.
- **Component 5 (Reasoned conclusion):** Met. The conclusion is stated conditionally consistent with the probable tier.

### Next Step

A user-assisted search of the Hamre parish marriage register at Digitalarkivet (digitalarkivet.no), covering approximately 1760–1800, remains the single most important next step. A positive result would verify the 25 June 1786 date (and record the exact place, witnesses, and parental names), potentially advancing the tier to proved. If the Hamre register is negative for this couple, the Hosanger parish fallback should be searched, and the discrepancy between the FGS claim and the register's absence would require resolution.

# Mentor review: proof-critique on ps_001

## What you've done well
You did exactly what the last review asked: the 1963 Family Group Sheet image is now actually open, and a_030/a_031 carry a genuinely stated marriage date rather than an unexamined stub. And the proof doesn't hide its own limitation -- the GPS Component Assessment section says plainly that Component 1 isn't fully met and names the exact missing source (Digitalarkivet's Hamre register). The narrative's hedging language throughout ('most probably,' 'preponderance of evidence') matches a probable tier honestly -- nothing here oversells.

## What to address before moving on
One thing matters before this goes in front of family: your narrative is careful to say the marriage *place* is only implied by the source's parish scope, not explicitly stated on the marriage line -- but the tree fact F4 records 'Hamre parish, Hordaland, Norway' as a flat, unqualified value, same as the explicitly-stated date. A family member reading the tree (not your prose) has no way to know the place is an inference rather than a document. I'd either set a lower confidence on that fact or attach a note carrying the same caveat your narrative already states -- the tree artifact should be as honest as the write-up.

## Worth considering
The tier move from not_proved to probable is defensible and the transparency about the still-unsearched Digitalarkivet register is good practice -- but that register (pli_008, and its Hosanger fallback pli_011) is still the one search that could confirm or overturn the specific date. When a user session is available, that's the search that gets you to proved.

## What would change my mind
Attaching a confidence marker or explanatory note to F4's place value so the tree doesn't claim more certainty than the source supports -- that closes the one must-address item here.
